description: We’re three fourth-year students combining computer science, software engineering, and medicine. Abdullah, Jafar, and Omar are developing Pulse Beyond , a tool that turns astronauts’ daily health notes into clear, reviewable check-ins. We aim to build a useful prototype grounded in NASA research.
summary:
When a crewmate reports sudden chest pain and ground support is delayed, the crew needs a clear way to ask for help and pass along what they know. We built Pulse Beyond, a tablet-first astronaut health reporting prototype for spacecraft, space stations, and lunar bases.

Crewmembers can report a concern about themselves or a teammate in their own words. Plain-language questions help them record what happened, enter available measurements, and mark what they’re unsure about. In urgent situations, the app prompts the crew to contact onboard help and prepares a handoff with the original report, available readings, and a timeline of actions. Mission settings let the crew record what equipment is available and whether support is reachable or delayed.

Pulse Beyond helps crewmembers without medical expertise give trained responders a clearer picture of what happened, what’s changed, and what still needs checking.
details:
Pulse Beyond is a tablet-first web app that helps astronauts report health concerns about themselves or a crewmate and pass clear information to trained support. We focused on what a crewmember without medical expertise can do when something feels wrong, especially when communication with Earth is delayed.

A crewmember starts by describing the concern in their own words. The app asks simple follow-up questions about when it began, what the person is experiencing, and where they are. The reporter can review the entry, mark anything they are unsure about, and save it. They can also manually enter blood pressure and pulse oximeter readings from separate devices or mark a reading as unavailable.

If a crewmate reports sudden chest pain, the urgent-help flow prompts the crew to contact onboard help through their mission channel without waiting for measurements. The crew can record what they observed, which actions they took or could not take, and what changed. The app organizes the available facts into an editable handoff and lets the crew export the stored record as JSON.

Our design preserves details that can get lost under pressure: the crewmember’s original words, the sequence of events, and what nobody could confirm. An unavailable reading stays marked as unavailable, so the next responder knows what still needs checking. The intended benefit is a clearer handoff when trained support is delayed or when another crewmember takes over.

We designed sample profiles for a spacecraft, a space station, and a lunar base. Crews can record equipment locations and support availability and see routine check-ins and reminders while the app is open. NASA’s Human Research Program informed our focus on distance from Earth and closed habitats. A fictional habitat timeline shows how observations and an environmental flag can overlap in time and location without implying a cause. We also included an interactive model from NASA/Ames as an ISS exterior reference.

We built the prototype with Replit Agent, React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. Three.js renders the ISS model. IndexedDB stores records in the browser, and a service worker caches the app and its assets for offline preparation. The app and presentation are hosted on GitHub Pages.

All 19 unit tests passed. We also checked the public Demo and Emergency pages and the 3D viewer. Pulse Beyond is a training prototype for reporting and handoff. Clinical review, device-specific measurement guidance, and testing on an installed tablet during a real network outage remain future work.
